item.title: New E-Bike Requirements May Cause Speed Bumps for Riders
item.author: The Frenchtown Sun
item.description:
This summer, the state of New Jersey began implementing new e-bike rules for all residents and visitors. All e-bike owners and renters should become aware of the new requirements.

Firstly, what is an e-bike? The law defines “e-bike” as both low-speed electric bicycles with a motor that only provides assistance while pedaling up to 20 miles per hour (mph) as well as motorized bicycles equipped with either a helper motor or an electric motor.

New Jersey requires that you must be at least 15 years old to operate an e-bike and have an e-bike license or a valid driver’s license. An individual may not apply for nor receive a motorized bicycle license if their driving privileges are suspended or revoked.

All e-bikes, including low-speed ones, must be registered with the New Jersey Motor Vehicle Commission (NJMVC). Visit www.nj.gov/mvc/vehicletopics/ebike.htm to make a NJMVC appointment, complete e-bike registration materials and learn more about the e-bike license process. Motorized e-bikes—not low-speed ones—are required to have insurance coverage and owners should secure insurance prior to NJMVC registration.

If you are looking to rent an e-bike in New Jersey, you must be at least 16 years old. Renters are not required to be in possession of a driver’s license or an e-bike license. Out-of-state visitors who bring their own personal e-bikes into New Jersey must comply with the state’s rules. This means they must be at least 15 years old, carry a valid license from their home jurisdiction, register the bike with the NJMVC and get insurance for a motorized e-bike.

The state law requires all e-bike riders aged 17 and under to wear helmets. However, several New Jersey municipalities have instituted more stringent e-bike requirements, including additional helmet regulations. Riders are encouraged to review local municipal e-bike rules before visiting. Visit njbikeped.org for detailed guidelines.

item.title: Frenchtown Advances Affordable Housing While Preserving Character
item.author: The Frenchtown Sun
item.description:
For decades, the borough has consistently embraced its responsibility to provide diverse, accessible housing options. Rather than viewing state affordable housing mandates as a bureaucratic hurdle, Frenchtown has historically approached affordable housing as an opportunity to strengthen the community from within.

In late June, in keeping with this long-standing commitment, the borough entered into a Consent Order and Final Certificate of Compliance and Repose approved by the Superior Court of New Jersey memorializing that Frenchtown met its Fourth Round affordable housing obligation (note: the Fourth Round housing obligation refers to the 10-year statewide affordable housing cycle—2025- 2035—mandated by legislation enacted in 2024). The Certificate of Compliance is a major milestone that secures the borough’s affordable housing adherence while pioneering creative solutions tailored specifically to Frenchtown’s unique character.

At its June meeting, the Borough Council adopted the final Implementing Ordinance and Resolution required to execute its updated Fourth Round Housing Element and Fair Share Plan (HEFSP).

By submitting these local enforcement laws to the New Jersey Superior Court, the borough satisfied its requirements under the state amended Fair Housing Act for the 2025–2035 cycle. The Certification formally secures the borough’s long-term immunity from developer-driven “builder’s remedy” lawsuits, protecting Frenchtown from high-density developments that may not fit the community’s scale.

Affordable housing in New Jersey is designed for low-and moderate-income households—often including working professionals who form the backbone of a community, such as teachers and first responders. Because the cost of living in Hunterdon County is higher than in many other parts of the state, local income eligibility levels are adjusted upward to reflect the regional reality.

While the state originally assigned Frenchtown a new construction obligation of 22 units, the borough successfully submitted a vacant land adjustment demonstrating that Frenchtown lacked developable land to absorb new high-density developments because of local environmental constraints such as steep slopes and flood plains. As a result, the state recognized a Realistic Development Potential (RDP) of zero for new construction. This crucial adjustment allows the borough to focus its energy on implementing innovative, small-scale housing solutions that honor the borough’s existing neighborhoods in keeping with its small-town, historic character.

To meet its remaining affordable housing obligation—including an 11-unit rehabilitation goal— the Borough Council and the Planning/Zoning Board designed a plan that looks inward rather than outward. Instead of relying on high-density development that could alter Frenchtown’s historic feel, the HEFSP introduces several forward-thinking initiatives funded by developer fees (not municipal property taxes):

  • The ECHO Unit Pilot Project: Frenchtown is introducing a pilot program for Elder Cottage Housing Opportunity (ECHO) units. These small, temporary, modular homes can be placed in the side or backyard of an existing single-family property. Partial funding for up to 5 ECHO units offers a flexible, compassionate option for residents to keep aging family members close by while preserving neighborhood aesthetics.
  • Mandatory Inclusionary Zoning Set-Asides: To ensure future growth blends naturally into the community, new residential developments will be required to integrate a percentage of affordable units directly into the development, maintaining the borough’s cohesive small-town aesthetic.
  • Local Neighborhood Rehabilitation Incentives: Dedicated funding will help up to 11 local property owners repair and update older, substandard units. This channels financial support directly to current households, preserving Frenchtown’s historic architectural charm while ensuring safe, code-compliant housing for neighbors of all income levels.

To fully back these innovative programs, the borough has also formalized the necessary state-required frameworks, including a structured Spending Plan for the developer-funded affordable housing trust fund, an Intent to Bond Resolution to serve as a financial backstop, updated Zoning Ordinances aligned with the borough’s local scale, and an Affirmative Marketing Plan to guarantee fair access to these opportunities.

The complete HEFSP and supporting documents are available for review on the borough’s website.

item.title: Frenchtown Literary Fest Attracting Prominent Authors
item.author: The Frenchtown Sun
item.description:
Frenchtown Bookshop’s first-ever Frenchtown Literary Festival kicked off with two events in June and continues on July 9.

The bookshop was awarded a $20,000 grant from American Express Shop Small, initially launched with a $5 million contribution to support 250 small businesses in honor of America’s 250th anniversary.

The festival, which is a series of author talks, presents “An evening with Ian Frazier” on July 9. A New Yorker essayist and humorist, he will speak in conversation with bookshop co-owner Barbara de Wilde.

He writes books of travel and history (Travels in Siberia and Great Plains) and hundreds of New Yorker pieces on topics that range from friendship, parenthood, and New York City to nature, human oddities, and the secret life of maraschino cherries. Ian Frazier is “one of the last inheritors of the great tradition of the New Yorker,” says editor Jonathan Galassi. He has twice won the prestigious Thurber Prize for American Humor.

A film adaptation of his article “Coyote vs. Acme” will be released this summer.

Tickets for his talk are $22.

This event, as well as the rest of events will be held in the Frenchtown School auditorium at 6:30 p.m., and the price of admission includes a signed copy of the featured book.

For more information, visit: https://www.frenchtownbookshop.com/literary-festival or call the Bookshop at 908-628-9297.

On Tuesday, Sept. 29, Eat, Pray, Love author Elizabeth Gilbert, will be launching the paperback edition of All the Way to the River: Love, Loss and Liberation, a harrowing and redemptive story of incandescent love, unspeakable tragedy and gradual return to health. Elizabeth calls Frenchtown “a wonderful, special community that has a Brigadoon-like feeling. It just doesn’t move at the pace of the outside world. It’s a special place.”

On Thursday, Oct. 1, Pádraig Ó Tuama, host of the podcast Poetry Unbound, will discuss his latest book of poems, Love Between Men.

item.title: Frenchtown’s 2026 Municipal Budget Approved—and Explained
item.author: The Frenchtown Sun
item.description:
Borough Council approved the municipal budget for 2026 on May 6. In New Jersey, municipal budgets are typically adopted later in the spring because municipalities must wait for finalized figures related to state aid, county taxes and other funding obligations before accurately completing the budget process.

The borough’s 2026 budget totals $2,886,272.08; Mayor Brad Myhre says that the budget reflects a continued effort to maintain essential services while remaining mindful of the affordability challenges facing residents. The most significant driver of increased spending this year was the sharp rise in employee health care costs. Local government employers participating in the New Jersey State Health Benefits Program (NJSHBP) are facing a substantial 36.2% premium increase for Plan Year 2026, creating added financial pressure for municipalities across the state. Brad notes that, despite these rising costs, the borough’s 2026 budget maintains staffing levels and includes only modest adjustments in other spending areas.

A municipal budget in New Jersey is a mandatory, legally binding annual plan that outlines how a town will raise and spend money. It sets spending limits, determines the municipal property tax levy, and allocates money for services like police, public works, parks and the library.

In New Jersey, municipal budgets are capped so that property taxes cannot be increased by more than 2% over the previous year, but there are some exceptions. Additionally, New Jersey municipalities may not increase spending by more than 3.5% over the previous year, with some exceptions.

The municipal budget is a financial blueprint divided into three primary sections. The Operating Budget covers the day-to-day “costs of doing business,” such as salaries for police and public works, trash collection, etc. Long-term investments for the borough’s infrastructure, like road paving and equipment upgrades, are managed through the Capital Budget, while the Debt Service portion is dedicated to paying the principal and interest on the funds borrowed to complete major projects. By balancing these three areas, the borough strives to ensure that current service needs are met while responsibly planning for the community’s future stability.

Understanding a municipal budget can be a challenging and complex endeavor; a few important pieces of background can help:

  • Sources of revenue: Local property taxes are the largest source of revenue contributing to the municipal budget. However, other revenue may include state aid; state and county grants for one-time costs such as transportation and parks projects; payments in lieu of taxes; fees, including sewer fees paid by borough property owners, other fees and permits such as building permits, marriage licenses, liquor licenses, and zoning fees; revenue generated from traffic violations and local ordinance infractions; and surplus funds from the previous year. Local property taxes fund 57.65% of this year’s budget, with 42.35% coming from those other sources. The borough’s chief financial officer indicates that the 2025 tax collection rate improved from 2024 and that the rate for 2026 is still inconclusive.
  • Municipal tax levy: It is important for readers to understand that the property tax rate is the total rate applied to a home’s assessed value, covering local, school, and county expenses, while the municipal tax rate is only the portion of that total rate specifically dedicated to fund the borough’s government services (such as police, public works, etc.).
    • In 2025, Frenchtown’s property tax rate was $2.731 per $100 of assessed value, which is generally in line with the Hunterdon County average of 2.72%. The tax rate for the 2026 budget cannot yet be determined while necessary information from schools and the county is still outstanding. About 24% of each resident’s total property tax bill goes toward municipal services (police, library, DPW, administration) while the remainder goes to the Frenchtown Elementary School, the Del Val Regional High School and county agencies.
    • The borough’s 2026 municipal tax rate is 0.6744 per $100 of assessed home valuation, representing an increase of 2.9 cents ($.029 per $100 of assessed valuation) over the prior year’s municipal rate. This represents an annual increase of approximately $103 on a home assessed at $350,000 or $133 on a home assessed at $450,000. As mentioned previously, the municipal tax rate represents borough services only. The borough’s budget remains in compliance with New Jersey’s 2% levy cap law, given several budget items that are excluded from the mandatory cap, such as debt service, pension contributions, some health care costs and certain emergencies.
  • Municipal spending: Total spending in the recently approved 2026 municipal budget is $2,886,272.08. The borough’s operating budget remained roughly flat (excluding grants and increases in health care costs) and the capital budget remained flat for 2026. Debt service increased 1.6% in 2026 due to bond anticipation notices for several borough infrastructure projects.
  • Who does what: Several important officials contribute to the development and management of the borough finances:
    • The Chief Financial Officer, JANET PRIVETTE, manages the municipal treasury. She is responsible for developing the annual budget and ensuring all spending complies with strict New Jersey laws. She oversees long-term debt. Janet can be reached at: cfo@frenchtownboro.gov or by calling (908) 996-4524 – Option 3
    • The Tax Assessor, ERICA BRANDMAIER, determines the fair market value of every property in the borough to ensure that the tax burden is distributed fairly. She is responsible for maintaining property records and tax maps, processing property transfers and deeds, reviewing applications for tax exemptions or deductions (such as those for seniors, veterans or non-profits), and defending assessments during tax appeals. Erica holds office hours at Borough Hall on the first Monday of each month, 5:30-7 p.m. She can be reached at: ebrandmaier@frenchtownboro.gov or calling (908) 996-4524 – Option 4.
    • The Tax Collector, ANNE MARIE SILVIA, is responsible for calculating individual tax bills based on the assessment and the current tax rate, mailing out the quarterly tax bills, processing payments and managing interest on delinquent accounts, and conducting tax lien sales if taxes remain unpaid. Anne Marie Silvia holds office hours at Borough Hall on Mondays, 5:30-8:30 p.m. with appointments available upon request. She can be reached at: taxcollector@frenchtownboro.gov or by calling (908) 996-4524 – Option 5.

The municipal budget story is ongoing, and The Sun will provide updates and clarification as we receive more information throughout the year.

item.title: Frenchtown Mourns the Loss of Rick Epstein, Historian, Author and Founder of The Sun
item.author: The Frenchtown Sun
item.description:
It is with the heaviest hearts that the editorial team of The Frenchtown Sun shares the loss of one of our founders, Rick Epstein.

The Frenchtown Sun was born out of a desire for more local news and Rick joined early conversations to develop our current newsletter iteration. He named The Sun and provided editorial content and suggestions up through our June issue, shortly before his passing.

The only one of us with editorial experience—and extensive experience at that—Rick was our guiding light. He would (very gently, as was Rick’s way) chide us for “spinach” content—pieces that lacked a human-interest element or intriguing hook. At every editorial discussion, we find ourselves asking, “What Would Rick Do?” His wisdom and guidance continue to provide support for The Sun.

On page 7, readers will find Rick’s obituary. While it details his amazing, adventurous life, it is hard to capture the spirit, humor and kindhearted-ness of a man who gave so much to Frenchtown—from his early years as a local reporter to his walking tours and history books. Rick’s last book is in support of the Frenchtown Elementary School Centennial, held later this month at FES, and covers the history of the school and its students.

As a community, we mourn and celebrate Rick who gave so much to this town. We encourage readers of The Sun to celebrate the life and legacy of Rick by being curious, thoughtful and kind.

item.title: Frenchtown Elementary School Will Celebrate Alumni and Community at Centennial
item.author: The Frenchtown Sun
item.description:
On Saturday, September 26, Frenchtown Elementary School (FES) will commemorate its centennial. Alumni and members of the community are invited to attend the festivities, which will feature the opening of the time capsule behind the building’s cornerstone, remarks by local leaders and a presentation on a forthcoming history book by local historian Rick Epstein. The celebration is free and open to the public. More information can be found at frenchtownschool.org/article/3005260. To support the celebration, commemorative merchandise is available for purchase online at FES Centennial Gear: spcustomgear.store/frenchtowncentennial. Frenchtown Elementary School Will Celebrate Alumni and Community at Centennial

In recognition of this historic milestone, The Frenchtown Sun met with two FES alumni—Wayne “Wink” Hummer (Class of 1962) and David “Dave” Gano (Class of 1961)—to celebrate their more than 75 years in the borough and their rich history with the school.

Dave Gano and Wink Hummer, approx. 5 years old (left); Wink Hummer and Dave Gano in front of FES in 2026 (right)

At 79 years old, Wink Hummer has lived in Frenchtown his entire life. He grew up on 3rd Street and married his wife, Ruth, in 1973. After renting a home on 2nd Street, the couple bought their current home on 4th Street in 1978.

Wink has five brothers, all of whom went through the Frenchtown school system. At the time, students attended kindergarten, 1st and 2nd grade at Borough Hall before moving to the Frenchtown School building, which housed 3rd through 8th grade.

Wink loved his experience at FES and fondly recalls his favorite teacher, Mr. Puperwinkle, who taught 1st and 2nd grade.

Unfortunately, in the 3rd grade, Wink contracted scarlet fever, causing him to miss six months of class. Following his illness, his mother requested that the school hold him back a year to catch up.

Later in middle school, Wink became a three-sport athlete, playing basketball, baseball and tackle football. After graduating from Frenchtown in 1962, he entered his freshman year at DVRHS. Keeping up the tradition, Wink and Ruth’s daughter and son also graduated from FES and attended DVRHS.

Dave Gano has lived in Frenchtown for 77 years, moving to the borough at just one year old.

Like Wink, Dave attended kindergarten through 2nd grade at Borough Hall and graduated from FES in 1961. He lived in various homes on 2nd and 3rd Streets until he was 38. He married his wife, Mel, in 1978, and they purchased their 8th Street home in 1981. Dave represents one of three generations of his family to attend FES—both of his daughters and his father went through the school system.

Dave played baseball and the tuba throughout middle school, frequently hauling the heavy instrument back and forth between home and school. He fondly remembers competitive recess games of kickball and dodgeball behind the school, back when the yard had no playground equipment.

Always a Terrier!

—Amelia Rodriguez

item.title: Worst Tick Season in a Decade is Predicted
item.author: The Frenchtown Sun
item.description:
Experts are warning that 2026 is turning out to be the worst tick season in 9 years, and New Jersey is right in the thick of it. The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) reports that early-spring emergency room visits for tick bites have reached their highest levels since 2017.

To stay safe this season, Frenchtown residents should be “tick-aware” and follow these essential precautions:

  • Wear light-colored clothing so ticks are easier to spot and tuck your pants into your socks.
  • Thoroughly check yourself, your children, and your pets upon coming indoors.
  • Stay on the path: Keep children and pets from running into underbrush along walking trails.
  • Use repellent: The CDC recommends using repellents registered with the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency containing DEET, picaridin, IR3535, Oil of Lemon Eucalyptus (OLE), para-menthane-diol (PMD) or 2-undecanone. For more information, see: https://www.cdc.gov/ticks/prevention/index.html.

To learn more about ticks and watch a step-by-step video on how to properly remove them, visit https://extension.rutgers.edu/tick. Additionally, scientists at the Rutgers NJ Ticks 4 Science program are asking residents to send in ticks they encounter which will be used to create a real-time tick tracking map. To learn how to mail in a tick, visit ticks.rutgers.edu.

item.title: Madison Rose Finery Opens on Bridge St.
item.author: The Frenchtown Sun
item.description:
Madison Rose Finery is the new boutique at 22 Bridge St., a space formerly occupied by the Sublime gift shop.

Gemologist and designer Madison Rose Whitman offers fine antique and estate jewelry, responsibly sourced gemstones, and an ever-evolving collection of handmade art and gifts. The shop provides a full range of jewelry services, including custom design, repair and restoration, appraisals, estate buying, consignment, expert consultations, and rare object sourcing.

“The boutique blends expertise, artistry, and storytelling, offering both locals and visitors a place to find meaningful gifts, celebrate milestones, or simply wander and be inspired,” says Madison Rose. “Drawing on a deep passion for gemology, natural history, and the wonder of discovery, the showroom is a quietly enchanting space where curious objects blur the line between adornment and artifact.”

Madison Rose delights in uncovering the details that bring pieces to life, whether identifying an obscure maker’s mark, interpreting the unique inclusions of a gemstone, or answering the question, “Is this a meteorite?” She says, “I enjoy helping people discover what they have, and what those pieces could become.”

She feels that “adornment is one of the most beautiful ways to experience the world. There is something powerful about natural treasures shaped over time and brought to life by skilled hands. Sharing that with others is at the heart of what I do,” says Madison Rose.

Her email address is hello@madisonrosefinery.com.

item.title: Operation Blue Angel will help residents during medical emergencies
item.author: The Frenchtown Sun
item.description:
The Frenchtown Police Department, in partnership with the Age-Friendly Frenchtown Initiative, now offers Operation Blue Angel, a voluntary program designed to assist Frenchtown Borough residents who are at risk of a medical or life-threatening emergency and may be home alone, unable to get to the front door to open it for help.

The program allows first responders to enter a resident’s home without unnecessary delays or potential damage to windows or doors when someone is unable to answer the door.

Participants in Operation Blue Angel are provided with a free, secured lock box that is affixed near the front entrance of their home. A house key is securely stored inside the lock box, and a confidential access code is placed on file with the Police Department.

In the event of an emergency, a police officer will access the code and use the key to accompany medical personnel into the home.

To be eligible for Operation Blue Angel, Frenchtown residents must be at least 55 years years old or have a medical condition that could lead to incapacitation; live alone or are alone for extended periods regularly. They may complete the required application and liability waiver forms and designate an emergency contact person. Visit www.frenchtownpolice.com for the application and waiver or contact the Police Department at 908-996-4820.

item.title: Environmental Commission wants to control invasive vines with beetles
item.author: The Frenchtown Sun
item.description:
When you see leaves that look like this, you’re looking at trouble.

As the soil warms up this spring, seedlings of the invasive and terribly aggressive Mile-a-Minute vine (Persicaria perfoliata) will sprout. Also known as devil’s tail, giant climbing tearthumb, and Asiatic tearthumb, this vine grows extremely rapidly and can take over gardens and woodlands, overgrowing shrubs, trees and outdoor furniture and buildings.

Single plants can easily grow up to 25-feet-long or more in a single season. The almost perfectly triangular blue-green leaves are easy to identify, and the entire plant is armed with tiny, hooked barbs that will catch on clothing and skin.

How to control this plant? Pulling the seedlings when the plants are young is quite easy—although you might want to wear gloves to protect your skin from the barbs. A biological control agent, the host-specific Asian Weevil Rhinoncomimus latipes is available from the N.J. Department of Agriculture to combat this scourge. This beetle has been thoroughly researched and has been used to successfully manage Mile-a-Minute vine since 2004.

This beetle only feeds on Mile-a-Minute vine, weakening the plants and reducing their ability to set seed. Since this plant must grow from seed each year—decreasing the seed production is key to controlling it. The Environmental Commission is seeking funds to purchase some of these beetles with the intention of releasing them at the Frenchtown Preserve to help control Mile-a-Minute vine there. —Randi Eckel

item.title: Updates from Borough Council
item.author: The Frenchtown Sun
item.description:
At its monthly meeting on August 5, Borough Council conducted the following items of business:

  • approved an ordinance to revise the Borough Code to allow the Environmental Commission to have two alternative positions;
  • approved a capital ordinance for various borough improvements, including costs to upfit a vehicle currently owned by the borough to make it “patrol ready” for the Police Department, a new vehicle for day-to-day operational use and renovations to Borough Hall;
  • authorized the preparation and submission of grant applications to the Large Foundation of Flemington, NJ and the Astle-Alpaugh Foundation to fund the operations of Age Friendly Frenchtown;
  • received several bids for the Pump Station and Department of Public Works (DPW) facility generator project. Power and Prestige Inc. in Newton, NJ will be awarded the contract;
  • appointed Carole Pepe as a part-time, as needed, library assistant and authorized the acceptance of a student volunteer to perform volunteer services for the borough;
  • acknowledged that the DPW erected a new flagpole outside Borough Hall with financial support from the Fargo Family Foundation;
  • shared that the town administrator and borough engineer had a pre-construction meeting with Comcast. Comcast will be installing three structures around the borough, in the right of way on Hawk St., Maple Ave. and Railroad Ave. to bring fiber connectivity to Frenchtown;
  • announced that street sweeping is tentatively scheduled for September 1 from 7 a.m. – 9 a.m. Parking will be restricted briefly on Race St. and Bridge St. No vehicles need to be moved in the residential areas;
  • announced that tax bills are now available online although paper copies are also available at Borough Hall if you have not received your mailed copy. The State of New Jersey was late in providing the borough approval, so tax bills were sent out late. There will be an extension until September 4;

item.title: Planning Board Considering Tightening Data Center Regulations
item.author: The Frenchtown Sun
item.description:
Data centers and their impact on communities have been featured prominently in the news across the country. On May 27, Gov. Mikie Sherrill announced a comprehensive statewide plan to address the impact of data centers on local communities.

The Frenchtown Planning Board will be considering the need for any changes to the borough ordinance regarding data centers. item.title: Frenchtown Elementary School Leadership
item.author: The Frenchtown Sun
item.description:
KATE NUGENT has served on the Frenchtown Board of Education for 20 years, and as president for most of that time. Frenchtown has a seven-member elected board whose job is to ensure that the school is well run. Their duties include setting district policies and goals, overseeing the budget, hiring and evaluating administrators, and serving as the communications link between the community and the school. As president, Kate is the primary spokesperson for the board. She ensures that meetings are conducted efficiently and works closely with the superintendent to discuss long-range plans. Kate and her husband have lived in their home on Third Street since 1995 and have raised four children who all attended Frenchtown Elementary School and Del Val High School.

Jim is a graduate of Del Val High School who spent nearly the first 20 years of his career working in a private special education school, serving and supporting students with multiple disabilities. Now in his seventh year at the Frenchtown School, Jim is most proud of the dedicated Frenchtown School team, as well as the many meaningful community relationships he has built throughout his time in Frenchtown.

item.title: Letter from the editor
item.author: The Frenchtown Sun
item.description:
I moved to Frenchtown in the early months of the COVID-19 pandemic. What I thought would be the beginnings of a charming life in a colorful small town was instead full of distance and isolation. Despite this bleak beginning, Frenchtown has demonstrated again and again over the last six years that we are a community of generous support, value and friendship.

Whether it’s chatting with neighbors on my front porch, waving to visitors on the path during a midday run or bumping into friends old and new during Riverfest, our little hamlet on the river has become my most treasured place: my home.

During an Age-Friendly Initiative survey conducted last year, we learned that residents want to feel more connected to their community and weren’t always clear where to get important information about what was happening in the borough. I hope that this monthly newsletter helps residents feel a sense of belonging with this special town.

Everyone must start somewhere, and I dream that The Frenchtown Sun will grow over time to be a meaningful contribution to our community. I hope you will join me on this journey to share all that this magnificent borough has to offer.

—Maria Whelan

item.title: Meet the Frenchtown Police Department
item.author: The Frenchtown Sun
item.description:
Each of Frenchtown’s police officers is devoted to a community‑centered style of policing, focusing on being approachable, engaged, and connected with the people he serves. They value the close connections that define small-town policing and take pride in being part of a department whose daily work is guided by compassion for our residents.

From left to right: Ptl. Kevin Coletta, Ptl. David Lugo, and Sgt. Erik Eccles

SGT. ERIK ECCLES has served as the officer in charge of the Frenchtown Police Department for the past six years and is nearing a decade of dedicated service to the borough and its visitors.

Erik oversees a wide range of operational and administrative responsibilities, ensuring that daily functions run smoothly while supporting long‑term organizational goals. He earned his bachelor’s degree in National Security Studies from New Jersey City University, graduating summa cum laude.

Off-duty, he enjoys caring for animals and has a genuine passion for their wellbeing. He jokingly refers to himself as a part‑time zookeeper, sharing his home with four cats and one dog.

PTL. KEVIN COLETTA has served with the FPD since 2019. Before that, he was a special law enforcement officer with Hackensack and Guttenberg police departments and the Essex County Sheriff’s Office.

Kevin’s responsibilities include serving as domestic violence liaison, juvenile liaison, Law Enforcement Against Drugs instructor, Megan’s Law designee, Traffic Officers Association representative, Firearms and Background investigator, fleet manager and field training officer. He is also the PBA Local 188 representative and its executive board secretary.

Beyond policing, he has volunteered in the fire service since 2014 and currently serves as assistant chief and president of his local fire department. He is a husband and father of two young children.

PTL. DAVID B. LUGO previously worked in Lambertville, where he developed a strong foundation in community policing and public service. His work there shaped his appreciation for building relationships and supporting the needs of local residents.

Outside of his duties, he enjoys spending time outdoors and has a lifelong love of animals and nature. David is grateful to serve a community he respects and enjoys being part of each day.

item.title: Updates from Borough Council in April
item.author: The Frenchtown Sun
item.description:
Borough Council meets on the first Wednesday of each month at 7 p.m. Meetings are open to the public, and they are also live-streamed at: https://frenchtownboro.com/livestream. The agendas for upcoming council meetings and minutes from past meetings can be found on the borough website.

At its April 8 meeting, the council introduced a resolution to adopt the annual municipal budget for 2026. This resolution will be acted upon at the council’s May 6 meeting. Other resolutions that were approved by the council include:

  • Hiring the street-sweeping services of the City of Lambertville.
  • Authorizing the borough’s participation in the Hunterdon Area Energy Cooperative Energy Aggregation Program. Frenchtown residents will be automatically enrolled, but they can opt out by returning a response card that is being mailed to each home. The program uses bulk purchasing to provide lower rates to consumers. For specific deadlines, detailed rate comparisons, or to manage your enrollment, visit the official HAEC website at https://njaggregation.us.
  • Authorizing the borough’s Environmental Commission to apply for a grant from the Association of New Jersey Environmental Commissions. If approved, the grant would provide funds for our Environmental Commission to host a community event to educate residents about local stewardship and invasive species management as well as to use a particular kind of beetle on borough public lands and parks to manage an invasive vine called “mile-a-minute.”
  • Authorizing a pilot program for the Frenchtown Sun and to apply for a grant from the Fargo Family Foundation to support it.

The council approved ordinances that:

  • Authorize conditions for filming in the borough. The ordinance is consistent with the state’s Film Ready program, which is designed to help production companies connect with municipal officials;
  • Establish the salaries and wages for borough employees for 2026;
  • Approve the start of Creek Road improvements using a $410,000 grant from the state Department of Transportation.

Also at the April 8 council meeting, Parks Commissioner Bill O’Brien updated that the borough has received a grant from the county to purchase and install modular skatepark equipment in Borough Park in early summer.

Frenchtown Borough residents are reminded about the following:

  • Property tax and sewer bill payments are due May 1. Payments can be made online, dropped off at Borough Hall or mailed in. If you have questions, contact clerk@frenchtownboro.com.
  • The borough is still taking comments from residents on a draft plan for the 71-acre Thompson Tract located on Creek Road near Borough Park. The tract was preserved in 2023 for passive recreation. The draft plan can be found online and residents are welcome to offer comments by emailing them to clerk@frenchtownboro.com.
  • Brush disposal and recycling in the Department of Public Works yard is available to borough residents and requires a permit.
    Landlords are required to make permits available to their tenants. All residents receive a DPW permit with their annual tax bill. Residents who did not receive or cannot find their permit may request one at Borough Hall by calling the clerk at 908-996-4524. A permit should be displayed on the vehicle’s dashboard when visiting the DPW yard. The drop-off hours for brush disposal are the second Wednesday of the month, 8 a.m. – 3 p.m., and the last Saturday of each month 9 a.m. – 12 p.m. Materials that are not allowed include: treated lumber, non-compostable materials, including stones and metals.
  • The Frenchtown Community Garden is a beautiful and productive space for borough residents. While all plots are already reserved for this year, borough residents may apply for a plot for next year; plots are assigned on a first come, first served basis. The application can be found on the borough website.
  • LINK buses offer free transportation to all residents. LINK has fixed bus routes, for which no reservation is needed. For areas in Hunterdon County not on a bus route, LINK offers curb-to-curb service weekdays, 7 a.m. – 5 p.m. on a first-come, first-served basis. Learn more at https://ridethelink.com.

item.title: Age-friendly Frenchtown
item.author: The Frenchtown Sun
item.description:
Borough Council will vote whether to endorse an Age-Friendly Action Plan at the June 3 meeting. The plan is the result of a year-long effort supported by a grant from the state Department of Human Services. The Action Plan can be found on the borough website. The next step is to send it for review by the state.

Valuable information collected as part of Frenchtown’s Age-Friendly initiative includes the following:

  • Frenchtown residents over the age of 55 comprised 16.7% of the total population in 1990. This population has more than doubled to 35.8% by 2020.
  • The median year that structures were built in Frenchtown is 1938 compared to 1979 for Hunterdon County and 1970 for the state. Many older residents have talked about the need for home renovations that will allow them to “age in place.”
  • The median income for Frenchtown residents 65 and older is $67,596 compared to $90,843 Hunterdon county-wide.
  • The percentage of Frenchtown borough households that are rentals is 47%. At recent Mayor’s Age-Friendly Town Hall meetings, residents have commented on the need for actions that ensure that older rental residents are living in homes that are healthy and safe.

item.title: Much-anticipated improvements coming to Harrison Street sidewalks
item.author: The Frenchtown Sun
item.description:
After more than a year of coordination with property owners along Harrison Street, all required access agreements have been secured, clearing the way for long-awaited sidewalk improvements. The project will include resetting existing pavers to eliminate tripping hazards and upgrading non-compliant ADA ramps to improve accessibility for all residents.

The Borough of Frenchtown was awarded a 2016 Safe Routes to School grant totaling $472,000 through the North Jersey Transportation Planning Authority to support this effort. While these grants typically move from award to construction within five to seven years, this project faced additional delays due to stringent federal requirements, the COVID-19 pandemic, and the time-intensive process of securing access agreements from all adjacent property owners.

The project is expected to go out to bid this spring, with construction scheduled to begin at a time that minimizes disruption to Frenchtown Elementary School. Once complete, these improvements will enhance pedestrian safety and accessibility along a key corridor in the Borough.

item.title: Frenchtown is getting “age-friendlier”
item.author: The Frenchtown Sun
item.description:
In March 2025, Frenchtown received a $70,000 grant from the state Department of Human Services to build community partnerships, assess the needs of our older residents, and create an “age-friendly” action plan. That plan is expected to be on the agenda at the June 4 Borough Council meeting.

The age-friendly effort is led by AARP nationally to help communities become more livable for the elderly. Frenchtown is already considered age-friendly, scoring 61 on AARP’s national Livability Index. The nationwide average score was 50. But we could be even friendlier.
More than 45% of households in Frenchtown include at least one person age 60 or older; the median income of residents age 65+ is $67,596 as compared to Hunterdon’s average of $90,843 for the same age group.

During the grant period, Frenchtown created an Age-Friendly Committee that updated borough demographics, created an inventory of services available to older residents, conducted a survey that received 206 responses, held listening sessions with key stakeholders, and hosted two town halls with significant participation.
The community-needs assessment found that:

  • Older residents feel a sense of “not belonging” within the community and have limited access to information about news, civic happenings, and social opportunities, which seems to stem from the absence of a local news source.
  • The county offers plenty of programs and services for older residents, but there are fewer programs within the borough and limited awareness of them.
  • A “community connector” would increase the availability of services and programs in Frenchtown by serving as a “match maker” between local volunteers and older residents with specific needs such as home repairs, transportation, and food delivery.
    The borough government could consider the needs of older residents with regard to home renovations to support aging-in-place, promoting repair of sidewalks to support walkability throughout the borough, ensuring the safety and livability of the approximately 48% of Frenchtown’s households that are rentals, improving parking downtown especially near Borough Hall and the library and strengthening the library’s ability to serve as a local “anchor” for all, including older residents and children.
  • The borough is poised to use two grants to improve sidewalks and pedestrian access.
  • That many residents and local organizations are eager to support age-friendly efforts, including the Frenchtown School, local businesses, churches, and service nonprofits.

To continue the age-friendly momentum, the state is allowing the borough to use its grant to implement several strategies that can serve as the foundation for ongoing age-friendly efforts. These include:

  • Launching the monthly newsletter that you’re reading now.
  • A free Operation Blue Angel program designed to assist Frenchtown residents who are at risk of a medical or life-threatening emergency. The program allows first responders to enter the home during a medical emergency without delays or causing damage. To read more about Operation Blue Angel or to sign up, go to: https://frenchtownpolice.com/. Contact Chris DeWire with questions.
  • Earmarking funds for the borough to consider changes to current ordinances that would reduce the cost and burden of obtaining local approvals for medically necessary home renovations that would facilitate aging-in-place.
  • Establishing a Constant Contact borough news service. See here to learn more.
  • Setting up a municipal trust that would allow the borough to seek funds to support creating an age-friendly community-connector effort.

On June 4, the Borough Council will consider the Age-Friendly Action Plan, and may modify it and may pass a resolution adopting it. Updates on Frenchtown’s age-friendly initiative can be found on the borough’s website at: https://frenchtownboro.com/community-services/age-friendly-frenchtown/.

item.title: Environmental Commission Hosts “Weevilpalooza” for all ages on July 3
item.author: The Frenchtown Sun
item.description:
The Frenchtown Environmental Commission will host Weevilpalooza on Friday, July 3 at 5:30 p.m. in the Frenchtown Preserve.

This is a family-friendly opportunity to learn about biological control of invasive species. Join commission members to release 1,000 weevils (Rhinoncomimus latipes) directly onto patches of the Mile-A-Minute vine (Persicaria perfoliata), an aggressive invasive plant that smothers native vegetation by blocking sunlight.

A biological control agent, these weevils have been thoroughly researched and have successfully managed the Mile-A-Minute vine since 2004. The weevil only feeds on the vine, weakening the plants and reducing their ability to produce seed and spread. Decreasing the seed production is the key to controlling it. Weevils were purchased from the state by a grant secured by the Environmental Commission.

People of all ages are invited to use hand lenses to observe the tiny weevils up close, participate in an invasive species scavenger hunt and take home a “Bug Scout” card explaining what to look for when they return to the Preserve to check on the weevils.

Participants should wear tick-protective clothing and gather for the event at the Frenchtown Preserve parking lot on Horseshoe Bend Road. Snacks will be provided and together, participants will walk to the release site. Due to limited parking in the lot, please consider carpooling.

For more information, please visit: https://frenchtownsun.net/redirects/weevils-info.

item.author: The Frenchtown Sun

The Frenchtown Planning Board has just begun a five-year review of the most recent master plan re-examination report (dated 2021).

What is a master plan? It is a blueprint for a municipality, outlining a vision for the future of the borough consisting of balanced economic, social, physical, environmental, and fiscal planning. While not a set of laws or regulations, a master plan provides guidance to the borough when making land use, zoning, and capital investment decisions.

The 2021 master plan re-examination report identified items to be addressed over the next 10 years, and the Planning Board will be discussing the borough’s progress on those items in the next few months at its monthly meetings at 7 p.m. the fourth Wednesday of every month, at Borough Hall (and streamed live).

item.title: Spotlight: Frenchtown Fire Department
item.author: The Frenchtown Sun
item.description:
Residents may have seen the Frenchtown Fire Department (FFD) supporting members of the community throughout the borough, including, most recently, during the July storm that caused significant tree damage and power outages in the area.

The FFD typically responds to 125-150 calls each year and there are currently 12 volunteers on the FFD roster.

Firefighting operations in the borough operate under a model that is intended to separate emergency operations from business or fundraising administration. Under this model, the FFD chief manages all on-scene emergency operations, training protocols, apparatus readiness and equipment procurement. The Union Fire Company, an independent, non-profit organization, manages facilities, organizational bylaws, finances and membership. Additionally, Frenchtown participates in a county-wide mutual aid agreement that includes municipal fire departments throughout Hunterdon and Bucks Counties. This agreement ensures a reciprocal system where Frenchtown and neighboring departments automatically dispatch extra firefighters, specialized equipment and emergency personnel to support one another whenever required.

The origin of Frenchtown’s dual model dates back to 1866. The department and the Vigilant Hose Company were established with 55 members, a hand pump fire apparatus and a hose cart with 500 feet of leather hose. After the Vigilant Company’s engine failed to operate during the 1878 fire that destroyed 25 homes and businesses downtown, the company disbanded.

In 1888, Borough Council members and citizens formed a committee to reestablish fire protection and on September 12, 1888, the Union Fire Company was formed, and the borough swore in fire department officers that day.

The firehouse structure located at 31 Second St. was purchased by the Union Fire Company in 1923 (the library occupies the original firehouse space).

Today, FFD volunteers must join both the fire department as well as the independent Union Fire Company. All volunteers must complete more than 200 hours of training.

The borough provides workers’ compensation insurance and the borough’s annual budget includes a line-item appropriation to the independent Union Fire Company of $26,000. The budget is spent directly on fire new equipment, equipment replacements, vehicle repairs and maintenance, training, materials and supplies. The Union Fire Company hosts fundraisers such as the recent Coin Drop; the proceeds of which go directly to the FFD budget. It costs $7000 to equip a single firefighter with basic gear; the FFD must provide an annual accounting of use of borough funds to the Borough Council. Additional budgetary line items pay for the utilities, fuel and insurances. The ownership of the fire trucks, life-saving equipment, and gear is split between the Union Fire Company and the Borough depending on how the assets were purchased.

Long-time Frenchtown resident, Mike Atheras, currently serves as the fire chief of the FFD. Chief Atheras is a retired member the New York City Fire Department and a former rescue specialist with New Jersey Task Force 1 Urban Search and Rescue. He was raised in Frenchtown and attended both Frenchtown Elementary and Delaware Valley Regional High Schools. Chief Atheras joined the FFD in 1988 and served as chief from 1996-2000. He took on the role again in January 2026.

Chief Atheras encourages residents to call 911 for emergencies rather than the FFD’s direct number, 908-996-4423, which is not monitored 24/7. Calling 911 ensures an immediate dispatch of the FFD alongside mutual aid partners.

Residents who are interested in becoming a volunteer member of the FFD can complete the application at: frenchtownfd.org/applications.

Residents who would like to be informed about operations of the independent Union Fire Company, can use the contact page at the FFD’s website: frenchtownfd.org/.

item.title: Frenchtown and Kingwood Methodist Churches to Merge and Become Open Door
item.author: The Frenchtown Sun
item.description:
Frenchtown and Kingwood United Methodist Churches will soon become the Open Door United Methodist Church, meeting at the Frenchtown church at 16 Third Street. Services will be on Sundays at 9 a.m. starting July 5 and will include a monthly dinner church service each month on third Sundays at 5 p.m.

Kingwood UMC is the oldest Methodist church in Hunterdon, and its site on Route 519 in southern Kingwood has hosted a church since the 1780s. At one time, the Kingwood church held several roast beef dinners a year that funded organizations such as rescue and fire squads, the Flemington Food Pantry, an animal rescue organization and more. In addition, Kingwood UMC has awarded over $50,000 in scholarships to Del Val High School students since 2019. Kingwood’s philanthropic spirit will be united with Frenchtown’s.

“I think of it as God at work creating something new,” said the Rev. Peter Mantell, pastor of the two churches, plus the Sergeantsville UMC, for the past 12 years.

The new church’s name was inspired by the Frenchtown church’s Open Door Food Pantry. “The pantry has become the focus of this church’s ministry and how the church has become identified,” Peter said, “so why not lean into that?”

The pantry started with a “blessing box” in the parking lot of the church the week of the Covid shutdown in March 2020. By that November, space was carved out of a corner of the church’s garage, making room for a refrigerator, freezer and shelves kept stocked with food.

It’s accessible around-the-clock. A cooking club of church members and volunteers was organized by Peter’s late wife, Anna, and the group continues to create and put out about 200 meals a week. Volunteers are always welcome Tuesday and Friday mornings between 9:30 a.m. and noon. Cooking skills are not required.

Donations of shelf-stable food are always welcome. Perennial pantry needs include shelf-stable milk, tomato products, peanut butter, jelly, cereals, no-sugar-added juices, soups, mac & cheese, canned tuna, canned chicken, canned vegetables and canned fruits.

Closing the Kingwood church was a difficult decision that has caused some sadness, but Peter said people are also hopeful for the future., looking to build relationships within the community, putting faith in action and making a difference in people’s lives. Meanwhile, plans are being made to remember and honor the long histories of the two churches.

“I’m very community-minded and try to bring that out in my preaching and teaching,” Peter said, “being inclusive, welcoming of all people, and helping the marginalized.”

The Open Door UMC will hold its opening service on Sunday, July 5, at 9 a.m. A local piano teacher, Kristen Todd, has been hired to help revitalize the music program, which will feature traditional hymns.

For more information, visit the website www.kingwood-frenchtownumchurches.com, call the Frenchtown church at 908-996-3117, or email Peter at pastorpmantell@gmail.com.

item.title: FES and DVRHS 2026 Budget Overview
item.author: The Frenchtown Sun
item.description:
In 2025, approximately 38% of Frenchtown’s property taxes funded the borough’s contribution to Frenchtown Elementary School (FES) and more than 23% went to Delaware Valley Regional High School (DVRHS) (see figure at left). While figures are not yet available for 2026, the two schools’ budgets are now finalized.

In New Jersey, public school districts cannot raise their property tax levy by more than 2% over the previous year without having available Statutory Spending Growth Limitation Adjustments or through voter approval.

FRENCHTOWN ELEMENTARY SCHOOL

FES’s total operating budget for the 2026/2027 school year is $3,237,340, with 40.5% going to classroom instruction, 9.8% to facilities management, 7% to administrative costs, 0.9% to transportation, 23.9% for employee benefits and 17.9% for specialized student support services (which includes the school nurse, speech therapy, etc.). The FES 2026 budget reflects a 1.69% increase in total spending from the previous year, which equates to a 2.0% increase in the property tax levy, matching the state 2% cap.

FES’s budget equals spending of $34,208 per student, compared to the statewide average of $28,822.

The district’s small student enrollment of 102 students provides a smaller student/teacher ratio and more individualized instruction. Per student administrative cost at FES is $2,069 per pupil, below the $2,172 state average for K-8 schools with less than 400 students according to the 2025 Taxpayers’ Guide to Education Spending.

Most of the increase over the 2025 budget is due to health benefit premium increases and specialized instructional support lines. Local property taxes contribute 80.4% of the total 2026/2027 budget, with state aid contributing 11.6% towards the total budget. This state aid represents a $28,919 increase from the 2025/2026 budget. Other sources of funds come from federal grants ($87,570) and state preschool grants ($486,855).

DELAWARE VALLEY REGIONAL HIGH SCHOOL

DVRHS’s total operating budget for 2026/2027 is $20,835,788, with 28.3% going to classroom instruction, 9% to facilities management, 6.2% to administrative costs, 7.2% to student transportation, 21.9% for employee benefits, 13.8% for specialized student support services (guidance, health services, extra-curricular activities, etc.), 7.9% in tuition and 5.7% for athletic and co-curricular programs.

DVRHS’s budget involves spending $27,497 per student, compared to the statewide average of $29,978. This cost-efficiency is noteworthy given the district’s smaller regional high school enrollment (approximately 660 students in grades 9-12), which typically drives up per-pupil overhead costs. Per-student administrative cost at DVRHS is $2,185 per pupil, below the $2,238 state average for grade 9-12 regional high schools.

The DVRHS 2026/2027 budget reflects a 0.71% increase in total spending from the previous year. This equates to a 5.49% increase in the local tax levy. A majority of this increase goes toward health insurance premium increases, special education tuition and transportation. Local property taxes paid for 82.5% of the total 2026/2027 budget, with state aid contributing 7.1% towards operations. This state funding allocation represents a $83,000 increase from the 2025/2026 budget. Other sources of funds come from federal grants and tuition from out-of-district students.

item.title: Former ArtYard visiting artist to give Frenchtown’s “Jane Doe” a headstone
item.author: The Frenchtown Sun
item.description:
A careful observer, strolling through the Frenchtown Cemetery, might notice a small, metal, grave marker inscribed: JANE DOE. It has been there since 1996, but this summer it may be replaced with a headstone with her real name on it: Wendy Louise Baker.

On Oct. 26, 1991, the body of a teenage girl was found by hunters in Warren County just off Interstate 80 not far from the Delaware River. Due to decomposition, the authorities could not determine the cause of her death, but it was declared a homicide.

No corresponding missing-person report could be found, and although a drawing of her was widely circulated by the State Police, no one recognized her. Because of a large tattoo of tiger on her left calf, she became known as the Tiger Lady.

With no one claiming the body, Frenchtown’s undertaker Eddie Johnson arranged for her burial in the Frenchtown Cemetery in 1996.

In 2021 Andrew Sullivan, a visiting artist at ArtYard from Fair Oaks, Calif., learned about Jane Doe and visited her grave, “I would like to honor her by providing a gravestone to replace the current stake in the ground.”

Andrew explains, “I have tried my best to be a more loving and attentive person, to care for, not only the visible world around us, but the invisible one as well.”

Although Jane Doe had been unidentified for 30 years, the Warren County Prosecutor’s Office event-ually used DNA from a bone sample to figure out that the Tiger Lady was Wendy Louise Baker, age 16.

Wendy was raised by her stepmother until she ran away from Florida at age 15 before landing in Coatesville, Pa., where she had relatives. When she disappeared, they assumed she had run away again and was living her life elsewhere. Her cousin Cindy Baker said of Wendy, “I don’t want to say [she was] a lost soul, but she seemed like she was kind of bounced here, bounced there, you know.”

Wendy’s granite tombstone will cost about $750. Andrew said, “I am going to transport it across-country in my own car sometime in the latter half of June. It will be a pilgrimage!” —Rick Epstein

item.title: Early Freeze Harms Local Orchards, Including Nagy’s Peaches
item.author: The Frenchtown Sun
item.description:
Northern Red Oak (Quercus rubra) leaves the day after the freeze on April 22.

It seems like a long time ago, but back on April 21 of this year, Frenchtown experienced a record-breaking hard freeze (as low as 23°F) that has had some long-term consequences for farms, trees and wildlife in our area.

Many plants, including mature hardwood trees, had already leafed out and the new leaves simply froze in place. Oak trees, hackberries, and others had all or most of their young leaves completely frozen and killed. Even young acorns, hackberry “berries,” maple seeds, and many other tree and shrub fruits (critical for wildlife) were frozen and killed. Countless flowering trees, from apple, peach and cherry trees at local farms, to flowering dogwoods and redbuds in yards and woodlands, had their flowers or young fruits frozen and killed. Even blueberries and strawberry crops were hard hit.

Farmers across the state have said that they have never seen anything like it. Due to the devastating effects of the freeze, Gov. Sherrill applied for statewide disaster designation, which was approved by the USDA for all 21 counties in the state on June 10. This makes N.J. farmers eligible for low interest federal loans to help them recover.

Few fruit and specialty farms in our area escaped damage: Nagy’s Orchard, just south of town, has announced that they lost their entire peach and apple crops for the year. In the entire region, local peaches and apples, among other fruits, will be hard to come by this year.

What does this mean for the homeowner who doesn’t have a farm? Acorns and many other important sources of wildlife food will be in short supply this coming fall and winter, but for the most part, plants have recovered by now. Oaks and many other trees re-leafed out late this spring using their secondary buds.

However, this has put a lot of stress on trees that have already been under stress for the past few years due to our persistent drought status. If dry weather continues, remember that trees and shrubs need water, too, particularly as they recover from the April freeze. —Randi Eckel

Northern Red Oak (Quercus rubra) one month after the freeze.

item.title: Borough considering parking meters
item.author: The Frenchtown Sun
item.description:
Turnover of parking spaces in downtown Frenchtown continues to be a significant challenge, particularly as warmer weather brings an increase in visitors. On weekends, many people park in municipal lots to access the D&R Canal Path, often leaving their vehicles for the entire day without visiting local businesses. This limits availability for customers who are looking to shop, dine, and support the downtown.

To address this issue, the borough is actively discussing the potential implementation of parking meters—an approach successfully used in many comparable river towns—to encourage greater turnover of parking spaces.

In addition to improving access to downtown businesses, metered parking would:

  • Help ensure adequate funding for police coverage and EMS services during peak tourism months
  • Create a dedicated revenue stream for downtown beautification and ongoing maintenance
  • Shift a portion of the financial burden from residential taxpayers to visitors who utilize public parking

This is part of a broader effort to balance accessibility, economic vitality, and quality of life, particularly during the busy summer season.

item.title: You Won’t Be Able to Buy These Plants
item.author: The Frenchtown Sun
item.description:
On January 20th, the New Jersey Invasive Species Management Act (NJISMA) was signed into law after more than 20 years of planning and discussion among scientists, environmental organizations, the NJ nursery industry, land managers and other stakeholders. This new act lists 30 invasive plant species (currently) that are now illegal to propagate, import/export, sell, or advertise—in other words, no one will be able to buy and plant these species in NJ anymore.

Invasive species degrade ecosystems by outcompeting native vegetation, changing soil chemistry, increasing erosion and devastating wildlife habitat—some invasive species, such as Japanese Barberry, actually make areas more likely to harbor large numbers of ticks, making them a significant health risk to humans. A 1996 federal executive order defined invasive species as “alien species whose introduction does or is likely to cause economic or environmental harm or harm to human health,” making this invasive species management act good news for New Jersey. In fact, the passage of NJISMA brings New Jersey up to speed with neigh-boring states (most of which have had lists of prohibited invasive species for many years) and creates the state’s first comprehensive framework to tackle harmful invasive species now, and in the future as the list of species evolves over time. Some of the species on the current banned list are well known problems in our area, such as Callary Pear, Tree of Heaven, Porcelain Berry, Running Bamboo, Japanese Hop, and Multiflora Rose. Other invasive species which have been commonly used in land-scapes in recent years are also on the list and may come as a surprise to some people—Norway Maple, Mimosa, English Ivy, European Privet, and Chinese Silver Grass, to name a few. These, too, can spread rampantly and cause ecosystem devastation.

See the full list of currently banned species below, almost all of which can already be found spreading in and around Frenchtown (species present locally have been noted with an asterisk):

  • Norway maple (Acer platanoides)*
  • Tree of Heaven (Ailanthus altissima)*
  • Mimosa Tree/Persian Silk Tree (Albizia julibrissin)*
  • Porcelain Berry (Ampelopsis glandulosa var. brevipedunculata)*
  • Japanese Angelica Tree (Aralia elata)
  • Japanese Barberry (Berberis thunbergii)*
  • Japanese Clematis (Clematis terniflora)*
  • Autumn Olive (Elaeagnus umbellata)*
  • Weeping Lovegrass (Eragrostis curvula)
  • Winged Burning Bush (Euonymus alatus)*
  • English Ivy (Hedera helix)*
  • Japanese Hop (Humulus japonicus)*
  • Sericea Lespedeza (Lespedeza cuneata)*
  • European Privet (Ligustrum vulgare)*
  • Amur Honeysuckle (Lonicera maackii)*
  • Morrow’s Honeysuckle (Lonicera morrowii)*
  • Purple Loosestrife (Lythrum salicaria)*
  • Japanese Crabapple (Malus toringo)
  • Chinese Silver Grass (Miscanthus sinensis)*
  • Eurasian Mater-Milfoil (Myriophyllum spicatum)
  • Oriental Photinia (Photinia villosa)
  • Running Bamboo (Phyllostachys)*

To see the most up-to-date list of banned species, or for more information, visit the NJ Invasive Species Strike Team information page www.fohvos.info/invasive-species-strike-team/info-center/.

—Randi Eckel

item.title: In Memoriam: Rick Epstein
item.author: The Frenchtown Sun
item.description:
Rick Epstein, 75, of Frenchtown died at home on July 20.

Born in Syracuse, NY, Rick was raised in Lawrence Township and graduated from Lawrence High School in 1969 and from Syracuse University in 1973 with a bachelor’s degree in journalism.

He held his dream job as editor of the Delaware Valley News in Frenchtown from 1977-1984. After becoming a parent, he worked as a managing editor at the Somerset Messenger-Gazette in Somerville, the Green Brook-North Plainfield Journal and the Highland Park Herald. He spent six years as a copy editor at the Central New Jersey Home News before coming to the Hunterdon County Democrat in 1995 where he was managing editor for many years. Rick contributed reporting and photography through 2015. Instead of entering retirement, Rick worked as a full-time library aide at Delaware Valley Regional High School from 2016-2025, where he also gave presentations to the journalism and history students, and photographed school activities for his write-ups on the school’s social media channels.

He was the author of two books on local history: Frenchtown: Fires, Floods, Fads & Felonies! A Newspaperman Tells the Story of a River Town (Palmetto 2023) and More Frenchtown: When You’ve Read Frenchtown and Want More! (Palmetto 2025) published with funding from the Fargo Family Foundation. He enjoyed sharing stories of local history on his Frenchtown walking tours. Rick was also the author of Rookie Dad; Adventures in Fatherhood (Hyperion 1992) and The Right Number of Kids (McKenna Publishing Group 2003). His funny-dad column appeared in more than 150 parenting publications in the U.S., Canada and Australia.

A memorial service will be held in Frenchtown later this autumn. item.title: Zöe Tober wins school centennial essay contest
item.author: The Frenchtown Sun
item.description:
The winners of the Frenchtown School centennial essay contest are Zöe Tober, first prize; Joshua Sanchez-Quackenbush, second prize; and Rosalie Strasser, third prize. Zöe and Rosie are eighth graders and Josh is a seventh grader.

They were among nine students who wrote on the theme “The Next 100 Years,” under the helpful supervision of Frenchtown School’s Language Arts duo—teacher Beth McCann and aide Ken Nohe. Donated by an anonymous benefactor, $100 will go to Zöe, $50 to Josh, and $25 to Rosie.

The contestants made predictions and recommendations for the future of Frenchtown and of planet Earth. Personal ambitions were also shared. Some efforts were serious and others were touched with whimsy.

The students’ names were redacted so the essays could be judged “blind.” The judges were Morgan Taylor, owner of Country Chic and president of the Frenchtown Business & Professional Association; Scott Sheldon, co-owner of the Frenchtown Bookshop; and Rick Epstein, local history enthusiast.

“The quality of the essays was heartening,” said Rick, “and we’re going to include some of them in a book that will be a souvenir of the Frenchtown School’s centennial.”

Zöe wrote, “Frenchtown is a beautiful place to live, a town so full of love and joy. Why isn’t the rest of the world? Why do people hate? Why do we fight? I don’t know, but I do know that out of all the hatred in the world, it is usually caused by sadness. And once you start using this angry façade when you’re hurting, it can be hard to stop. That’s because it feels easier than talking through the feelings you’re experiencing.”

Her hope is that “one day the love in Frenchtown will spread to other communities, and keep growing from there until we have real world peace. As we move into high school, I challenge everyone here to be brave enough to choose talking over fighting.”

She urges, “Next time you see someone being mean, don’t just do it back. You need to help them correct their own behavior or it will never change. And I can’t stress this enough, but hate is rooted in sadness. You need to be an ally to the ones who are hurting, not an enemy. Peace starts now, it starts with you.”

KYLE J. ALLEGER 26, died on March 10 in Ewing Township as the result of an automobile accident.

He was the son of Joel R. and Sue Ann D. (Sliker) Alleger of Frenchtown.

Kyle was born June 4, 1999, in Princeton and grew up in Frenchtown.

He graduated from Delaware Valley High School in 2017. Kyle worked in the Logistics/Parts Department of Penske Truck Leasing in Burlington.

His dedication to his work was admired by his peers, and he took pride in being part of a team that emphasized efficiency and support.

Besides his loving parents and brother Colin, Kyle is survived by his maternal grandmother, Diane Campbell of Milford; his paternal grandmother, Agnes Alleger of Flemington; and several aunts and uncles, as well as many cousins who will cherish his memory.

His funeral was held on March 17 at HolcombeFisher Funeral Home in Flemington and interment was in St. Magdalen Cemetery, Flemington.

DENNIS B. CARR, 79, of Holland Township passed away on Feb. 17 at St. Luke’s Warren Hospital in Phillipsburg. He was president of the Frenchtown Cemetery Association for more than 20 years.

Born on Jan. 3, 1947, in Frenchtown, Dennis lived in Mount Pleasant before moving to Holland Township 50 years ago. He was a 1965 graduate of Delaware Valley High School.

Dennis was drafted into the Army in 1966 and was stationed in Germany. Afterward, he worked for the U.S. Postal Service for more than 30 years in Morristown, Flemington, Hillsborough, and South River, before retiring in 2001.

Dennis was a member of the Frenchtown American Legion and the Everittstown United Methodist Church, where he taught Sunday school, and served as a trustee. Dennis served his country, his community, and his church faithfully and with quiet dedication. Most of all, he was a dedicated and loving husband, father, and “Pop” or “Poppy” to granddaughter Kylee.

Son of the late William Carr Sr. and Cora (Pursell) Carr, Dennis is survived by his beloved wife of 54 years, Patricia A. (Rounsaville) Carr, his son Eric M. and his wife Nicole, his three brothers Harry, William Jr. and Theodore, his sister Sandra Lutz and her husband William, his granddaughter Kylee, his granddog Baylee, and many nieces, nephews, and friends.

A celebration of Dennis’ life will be announced at a later date. Interment will take place at the Frenchtown Cemetery. Its first show was Stagecoach, starring John Wayne. The photo on the left was taken in 1941. Nelverna Bellis, manager from the 1940s into the 1970s, was very strict. item.title: What WWII Troops Told the Principal
item.author: The Frenchtown Sun
item.description:
In the cellar of the Frenchtown School, there are many things, including 75 cardboard banker’s boxes. Most of them are filled with boring stuff like old invoices, audit reports, school-board meeting agendas and minutes, and personnel and student records.

But one of them contains a thick folder full of letters and postcards received by Principal Bert Light during World War II. He was in charge of the K-12 school in 1931-59, and was something of a father figure. He’d been an Army officer in World War I. So, some of his alumni, in uniform, wrote home to him.

Coast Guard Yeoman 3rd Class Charles Strouse (Frenchtown High School Class of ’42), stationed in Ketchikan, Alaska, wrote of “the most miserable weather I have ever had to experience. It is constantly raining, snowing or drizzly… The ground is muddy and it’s usually foggy.”

His classmate Vernon L. Wood of the Army Air Corps apologized for “griping” about Coach Miller’s tough workouts, which have been “of great advantage to me during the time I have been in the service.”

That coach, Bill Miller, then a lieutenant in the Navy, sent his former boss a three-page typewritten report on the sugar and pineapple crops on Oahu, Hawaii, the architecture of the schools there, and the style of high-school football played there. “They play a very open game and flip the old apple around like a basketball most of the time.”

John L. Case Jr. wrote from an Army air base in New Hampshire. He ask for a recommendation to be a flying cadet, instead of a clerk in a quartermaster company. But he praised his Frenchtown High School training, noting that “only about 30% of all clerks in the Army can really type the correct way.”

Infantry Pvt. Clarence Kirk, part of the Sicily invasion, was having a pleasant interlude in August of 1943. Sitting in the shade of an olive tree, he wrote, “The people were very glad to see us and said we should have come three years ago. There is plenty of fruit such as [indecipherable], lemons, figs, and some orange… We go swimming quite often and spend the rest of our free moments trying to talk to Italian fruit peddlers.” The only clouds in his blue sky seemed to be the low quality of Italian stationery and marching up the Sicilian hills.

Kenneth L. Blanchard (Class of ’44), a Seabee stationed on Okinawa, wrote in 1945 of Japanese air raids, and Eli E. Hager (Class of ’48) wrote in 1951 from the USS Walke, a destroyer stationed off northern Korea. He mentioned a time when his ship exchanged fire with a shore battery. His was the only letter from that war.

Most of the men were grimly determined to do their duty. But Pvt. Manuel Severs (Class of ’41) was jubilant. He wrote from Parris Island, S.C., in September of 1942, “I love the Marine life in every way” and vowed that if he survived the war, he would re-enlist. “We receive the best training of any soldier in the world. Therefore, we have full confidence in our selves and the weapons we use.” He achieved sharpshooter status with the .45 pistol and the .30-caliber 1903 Springfield rifle. “It makes me feel great to know that I will stand up before any enemy and know that I can fire my rifle better than he.”

He happily listed all the other firearms he learned to use, including the Browning automatic rifle, the Reising submachine gun, and the .50-caliber machine gun. But the new M-1 rifle was his favorite. It was “well-constructed,” easy to aim, and equipped with a clip of eight bullets, three more than the Springfield. He relished bayonet and grenade practice and the instruction in hand-to-hand fighting that made Marines more than a match for Japan’s best scrappers. He was also enjoying the “chow,” which was plain but plentiful. “I wouldn’t trade places with any man in the world,” he wrote.

None of the letter writers offered details of frontline combat, perhaps for security reasons, but they do give glimpses into a chapter of world history through letters that landed in the principal’s in-box.

By Rick Epstein, adapted from Terriers Forever!, a soon-to-be-published book commemorating the 100th anniversary of the Frenchtown School.

item.title: History Spotlight: The Fargo Family Foundation
item.author: The Frenchtown Sun
item.description:
For over a century, the Fargo family name has been deeply rooted in Frenchtown. As chronicled in Rick Epstein’s local histories, Frenchtown and More Frenchtown, the family’s legacy in the borough began with patriarch Clarence B. Fargo. Professionally, Clarence operated a printing and publishing bus-iness in Frenchtown, running a mail-order flower-seed and bulb business out of a commercial building on Bridge Street, alongside his work documenting local history. Beyond his business ventures, Clarence was an active community member who engaged deeply with the local area, eventually authoring the foundational History of Frenchtown in 1933.

The family’s deep commitment to civic life extended proudly through the generations. Clarence and his wife raised three daughters—Edith, Marion, and Marjorie—who lived in the family’s Frenchtown home for over a century.

Throughout their lives, the family remained dedicated to local development and community well-being. The Fargo sisters were especially committed to supporting the local community, contributing generously to local churches, emergency service providers and animal shelters, with a particular focus on the welfare of women and children.

To honor their father and ensure their lifelong dedication to the region endured, the sisters established the Fargo Family Foundation. Today, the Foundation continues to enrich the Frenchtown community by awarding grants that improve the quality of life for both people and animals throughout the Delaware Valley. From Clarence’s early preservation of our town’s stories to the foundation’s ongoing philanthropic impact, the Fargos remain an indelible part of the fabric of Frenchtown.

item.title: Frenchtown then & now
item.author: The Frenchtown Sun
item.description: The Hummer Building, as some of the old-timers call it, is on the left. The western half of it was built by druggist and liniment manufacturer Albert Williams right after the Great Fire of 1878 on the ashes of his former building. The original tenant on the corner was George W. Hummer’s furniture and undertaking business. Williams’ pharmacy was next door. Lorenzo Kerr put up the other half in 1881. His original tenant was DeWitt C. Dalrymple’s store, whose wares included corsets, men’s straw hats, lace curtains, feathers, and parasols. (Ten years later, Mr. Dalrymple was yardmaster of a Hoboken railyard and was run over by a train). The current owner is Jill Kearney, who also owns FiNNBAR. Although she is the founder and executive director of ArtYard, these are her personal holdings. —Rick Epstein

item.title: Frenchtown then & now
item.author: The Frenchtown Sun
item.description: THE ODD FELLOWS BUILDING at 17-19 Bridge Street is 47 feet tall, making it Frenchtown’s tallest. Completed in 1897, it was built for the Independent Order of Odd Fellows, Frenchtown’s most prestigious and affluent lodge. The lodge brothers, who were dedicated to doing good deeds, met on the third story. When the picture (below, left) was taken circa 1930, the lodge was still going strong. In the 2026 photo (below, right), the building is missing its next-door neighbor. Over the years, that brick residence was the home of Bridge Street merchants Hugh Warford (b. 1826-d.1887), Charles N. Reading (1854-1919), and Samuel Frenchtown then & now O. Eddy (1864-1934). It was saved from the Great Frenchtown Fire of 1878 by men with ladders, buckets, and strips of wet carpet. But in 1962 Wilbur Stout of Pennington bought it and let it decay, finally demolishing it in 1972. —Rick Epstein
